articles.title: Does CT seatbelt sign, traumatic abdominal wall hernia or body habitus predict injuries and patient outcomes following a restrained motor vehicle collision? A New Zealand cohort study.
articles.abstract:
**AIMS**: to assess for associations between CT seatbelt sign (CTSBS), traumatic abdominal wall hernia and central adiposity with the severity of injury and subsequent management following a restrained motor vehicle collision.

**METHODS**: Included patients were all major trauma patients (with an injury severity score ≥12), who were involved in a motor vehicle collision (MVC) and were restrained by a seatbelt, presenting to Christchurch Hospital between July 1st, 2018, and June 30th, 2023. Clinical data was collected prospectively by the Trauma team nursing staff at the time of injury and throughout the patient's admission. Original trauma CT imaging either performed at Christchurch hospital or the presenting hospitals were re-reviewed by a trauma specialist radiologist, as well as a post part 2 FRANZCR final year radiology trainee. The presence of a seatbelt sign, injuries and central adiposity were calculated from these images. Both univariable and multivariable analyses were performed.

**RESULTS**: After exclusions 316 patients were included in the study. For CTSBS, there was Statistically higher incidence and grade of organ injury in both the thoracic and abdominal compartments except for large thoracic and abdominal vascular injuries, spinal injuries and pelvic injuries. Multivariable analysis demonstrated 10.41 times higher rates of death when CTSBS is present albeit with just 11 deaths. Outcomes were also worse when CTSBS was present; Injury severity score (13% higher), number of operating sessions (15% higher), length of ICU stay (64% higher) and hospital stay (32% higher). Regarding traumatic abdominal wall hernias, there was a higher incidence of any intra-abdominal organ injury (p = 0.042), as well as a higher incidence of GI tract (p < 0.001) and mesenteric injuries (p < 0.001). Regarding central adiposity, there was no significant difference of any of the measured outcomes when looking at different central adiposity groups except for number of operating sessions (p = 0.012).

**CONCLUSION**: The presence of a CTSBS or traumatic abdominal wall hernias are associated with a higher rate of organ injury and worse outcomes. Radiologists should include these signs in their reports. Differences in central adiposity have no significant associations with outcomes as the result of a restrained MVC.

articles.title: When drowning surveillance misses the mechanism.

Total gastric and intragastric air volumes in immediate post-resuscitation whole-body computed tomography after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: Association with airway management, aspiration, diaphragmatic position and initial blood gas analysis.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Gastric distension (GD) may occur during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), but quantitative human data after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remain limited. We quantified gastric volumes after OHCA and explored associations with prehospital airway strategy, CT-defined aspiration, diaphragmatic position, and initial blood gases.

**METHODS**: This retrospective single-center study included OHCA patients undergoing post-resuscitation whole-body computed tomography (CT) within 180 minutes of emergency department (ED) admission between January 1, 2020, and March 31, 2025. Total gastric volume (TGV) and intragastric air volume (GAV) were quantified by CT volumetry.

**RESULTS**: Of 255 identified patients, 120 underwent CT within 180 minutes. Median TGV was 594 mL and correlated strongly with GAV (p < 0.001). Among patients with an advanced airway at ED arrival, neither TGV (p = 0.20) nor GAV (p = 0.24) differed significantly between the tracheal airway (TA; n = 87) and supraglottic airway (SGA; n = 28) groups. CT-defined aspiration was numerically more frequent with SGA than TA (78.6% vs. 57.5%; OR 2.7; p = 0.071), whereas neither TGV nor GAV was associated with CT-defined aspiration. Weak positive correlations were observed between initial pCO

**CONCLUSION**: Gastric volumes were high in this selected post-OHCA immediate CT (< 180 minutes) cohort. No significant differences were detected according to recorded prehospital airway strategy, and gastric volume was not associated with CT-defined aspiration. Mechanisms and clinical consequences remain uncertain and require prospective studies before preventive/ therapeutic implications can be established.

articles.title: Frequency of On-Scene Goal-Directed Field Interventions for Pediatric Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest in a Regional System of Care.
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVES**: Early on-scene resuscitation improves outcomes from pediatric non-traumatic out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA); however, for pediatric patients, the early evacuation strategy remains commonplace. We sought to determine the frequency of goal-directed interventions initiated by paramedics prior to transport for pediatric patients with OHCA in a regional emergency medical services (EMS) system.

**METHODS**: In this retrospective observational study and cross-sectional analysis, we analyzed the Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival (CARES) and linked electronic patient care reports (ePCR) data for patients aged <15 years treated by EMS for nontraumatic OHCA in Los Angeles (LA) County from January 2021 to December 2022. The primary outcome was the frequency of goal-directed therapies administered on scene prior to transport, which we defined as defibrillation for shockable rhythms and administration of epinephrine and fluid resuscitation for non-shockable rhythms. We also tabulated descriptive statistics regarding arrest characteristics, scene times, frequency of other prehospital treatments, and patient outcomes.

**RESULTS**: Among 176 eligible pediatric OHCA cases analyzed in CARES, 112 (64%) were male, the median age was 10 months (IQR 3-51), and 162 (92%) had an initial non-shockable rhythm. Of these, 156 patients were successfully linked to electronic patient care report (ePCR) records for analyses of prehospital interventions. Among 143 patients with non-shockable rhythms, EMS administered epinephrine before transport in 58 (41%) and fluids in 12 (8%). Among 13 patients with shockable rhythms, EMS delivered defibrillation before transport in 11 (85%). Bag-valve-mask (BVM) use was documented in 80 (51%) patients, although its timing relative to scene departure could not be determined. Median on-scene time was 10 minutes (IQR 5-18). Ten patients (6%) survived to hospital discharge, including 6 (3%) with a favorable neurologic outcome.

**CONCLUSIONS**: In this regional EMS system, fewer than half of patients with non-shockable rhythms received a dose of epinephrine and fewer than one in ten received intravenous fluids prior to transport, whereas most patients with shockable rhythms were defibrillated on scene. Further work is needed to identify barriers to timely delivery of on-scene resuscitative interventions.

articles.title: Prevention of fireworks-related injuries: a systematic review and practice management guideline from the Eastern Association for the Surgery of Trauma.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Fireworks-related injuries (FRIs) are an increasingly common and preventable problem worldwide. Fireworks have highly variable regulation, and yet there are no evidence-based guidelines for injury prevention.

**METHODS**: A priori Population(s), Intervention(s), Comparison(s), and Outcomes (PICO) questions were created. PICO 1 asked, "For children (age<18), should their interaction with fireworks be restricted to professional fireworks displays as compared to private fireworks use to reduce incidence of any FRI, rates of amputation, mortality, vision loss, and burns, and increase return to school or work after injury?" PICO 2 asked, "For both adults and children, should restrictive fireworks-related legislation, as opposed to more lenient legislation, be enacted to decrease the same outcomes?" A systematic search and review of the literature was performed, and the quality of evidence was graded per the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) methodology. Final evidence-based recommendations were developed with working group consensus.

**RESULTS**: No studies were included to answer the question related to professional versus private firework displays due to the lack of direct comparisons. Ten studies were identified to analyze the impact of fireworks-related legislation. Eight studies had positive results, suggesting that more stringent legislation of fireworks sale and use is associated with a lower incidence of FRI, and two studies showed no difference. Quality was deemed to be very low.

**CONCLUSION**: Although of very low quality, available data are consistent in showing that more stringent legislation is associated with a lower incidence of FRI. We therefore conditionally recommend restrictive legislation to limit the sale and use of Class C fireworks by non-professionals to reduce FRI. We cannot make any recommendations regarding private fireworks use because of limited available data, but it is important to note that very few reported injuries occurred at professional displays.

**LEVEL OF EVIDENCE**: Guideline; Systematic review, level IV.

articles.title: Feasibility of a prehospital point-of-care bioassay in patients with mild traumatic brain injury (GFAP-TBI): a pilot simulation study.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Rapid prehospital identification of intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) after traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains a challenge. Point-of-care (POC) bioassays of biomarkers of ICH, glial fibrillary acidic protein, and ubiquitin carboxyl-terminal hydrolase L1 offer promise for early detection of intracranial injury and improved triage and prehospital treatment decisions.

**METHODS**: We conducted a prospective pilot feasibility simulation study to evaluate operational implementation of a prehospital whole blood POC device (i-STAT Alinity, Abbott) performed by paramedics in Maryland. Emergency medical services (EMS) clinicians were trained to interact with physicians using a mobile communication platform, Pulsara, during a simulated prehospital encounter involving patients with mild TBI, Glasgow Coma Scale Score of 15, who would be eligible for a research protocol using the POC testing. Saline from a simulated IV was used in place of a blood draw. Time metrics were recorded, and participants completed postsimulation surveys assessing usability and workflow integration.

**RESULTS**: Twenty-four paramedics completed simulations. Median time for teleconsent was 2 (IQR 2-2.5) minutes, device data entry 1 (1-2) minutes, and blood transfer to assay 1 (1-2) minutes. Median total workflow time from consent initiation to assay completion was 6.5 (5-7) minutes. Survey responses demonstrated high usability, with over 90% of participants reporting that training was sufficient. The device was easy to operate, and the workflow could be integrated into routine EMS care. All participants indicated willingness to adopt the device in clinical practice.

**CONCLUSIONS**: In this pilot simulation study, prehospital teleconsent and implementation of a whole blood POC bioassay by paramedics were feasible within simulated EMS workflows and could be completed within typical transport intervals. These findings support further clinical investigation of biomarker-based triage strategies for patients with suspected TBI.

articles.title: Gram stain results provide reliable guidance for antibiotic decisions in a surgical trauma intensive care unit.
articles.abstract:
**INTRODUCTION**: The frequent use of broad-spectrum antibiotics and rising antimicrobial resistance in the intensive care unit (ICU) makes antimicrobial stewardship essential. Gram stain results have been used to guide initial therapy, but their role in de-escalation is less defined. This study evaluated the reliability of Gram stain results for early antibiotic de-escalation, hypothesizing that blood culture Gram stains are highly predictive compared with other specimen types.

**METHODS**: We conducted a retrospective diagnostic accuracy study of cultures from patients admitted to a surgical/trauma ICU during a 1-year period. Gram stain results were compared with final culture results to assess concordance. Specimen types with fewer than 20 samples were excluded from secondary analysis.

**RESULTS**: Of 319 patients, 109 (34%) had cultures collected (n=378). Blood (42%), lung (28%), and urine (21%) were most common. Overall, Gram stain results demonstrated 73% positive predictive value (PPV), 87% negative predictive value (NPV), and 84% accuracy. Blood cultures (n=157) had 100% PPV and NPV with 100% accuracy. Urine cultures were highly reliable for identifying infection (PPV 100%) but less so for ruling out infection (NPV 93%, accuracy 94%). Lung cultures showed poor predictability (PPV 44%, NPV 70%, accuracy 63%).

**CONCLUSION**: Gram stain results can support early antibiotic de-escalation in the ICU. Blood culture Gram stains are highly reliable, urine moderately so, while lung specimens are less predictive. These findings may inform antimicrobial stewardship strategies in critical care settings.

**LEVEL OF EVIDENCE**: Diagnostic tests-level III.

articles.title: Bedside electromagnetic neuronavigation for cranial access procedures in neurotrauma and neurocritical care.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Bedside cranial access devices (external ventricular drain (EVD), subdural evacuation port system (SEPS), parenchymal intracranial pressure (ICP) monitor) are foundational to neurotrauma and neurocritical care. Craniometric-based techniques are limited by aberrant anatomy, clot-filled ventricles, and complex extra-axial collections. Bedside electromagnetic (EM) neuronavigation registered to computed tomography (CT) imaging may enable precise targeting without requiring transport to the operating room, general anesthesia, or rigid cranial fixation.

**METHODS**: We retrospectively reviewed patients undergoing bedside cranial procedures with EM-neuronavigation (Medtronic StealthStation) from November 1, 2025 to July 21, 2026 at our Level I trauma center neurocritical care unit for distorted anatomy, atypical targets, and/or high consequences of imprecision. Outcomes included device function, post-procedure neuroimaging confirmation of device placement, and navigation-related complications.

**RESULTS**: Ten patients underwent 15 EM-navigated bedside procedures (11 EVDs, 2 SEPS, 2 parenchymal ICP monitors). Clinical indications included aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, traumatic brain injury, loculated subdural hematoma, ventriculitis, ventricular trapping, obstructive hydrocephalus, and intracerebral hemorrhage. Notably, EM-navigation enabled dual-catheter placement to access non-communicating ventricular compartments and optimized SEPS placements at maximal extra-axial collection thickness while avoiding vascular membranes. All procedures achieved intended device function and intended positioning on post-procedure imaging. There were no complications or revision procedures related to EM-navigation.

**CONCLUSIONS**: In this single-center proof-of-principle series, bedside EM-navigation was feasible, safe, and readily integrated into high-risk patient care workflows in neurocritical care. Whether bedside neuronavigation improves procedural precision, supports clinician education, or reduces operative and transport needs was beyond the scope of the current study and requires well-designed prospective evaluation.

**LEVEL OF EVIDENCE**: Level V, Therapeutic/Care Management.

articles.title: Accountability in emergency surgery: moving beyond blame toward high reliability: a WSES-JMESE position paper.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Emergency surgery is characterized by clinical uncertainty, time pressure, evolving information, physiological instability, and substantial variability in available resources. In this setting, adverse outcomes may occur despite timely and appropriate care and should not automatically be interpreted as evidence of professional failure. Nevertheless, surgeons may be exposed to retrospective, outcome-driven, and overly individualized attribution of blame when the complexity of the original decisional environment is insufficiently considered. A structured framework is therefore needed to support fair, proportionate, and learning-oriented accountability in emergency surgical practice.

**METHODS**: This evidence-informed position paper was developed through a structured multidisciplinary review of literature from patient-safety science, cognitive psychology, medical ethics, health-systems research, surgical professionalism, and high-reliability organization theory, complemented by iterative expert discussion within the World Society of Emergency Surgery-Journal of Medical and Surgical Errors working group. The literature was synthesized narratively to identify the principal contextual, cognitive, ethical, professional, and organizational domains relevant to fair accountability and adverse-event review in emergency surgery. The resulting statements were framed as ungraded evidence-informed Good Practice Statements according to the GRADE framework rather than clinical practice recommendations based on comparative effectiveness evidence.

**RESULTS**: The synthesis identified seven interrelated principles for fair accountability in emergency surgery: contextual proportionality; distinction between accountability and blame; mitigation of hindsight, outcome, and attribution bias; recognition of distributed responsibility across individuals, teams, and systems; protection of professional integrity; procedural fairness and institutional responsibility; and application of high-reliability principles. Particular attention is given to the dynamic and time-dependent nature of emergency surgical decision-making, the incomplete representation of clinical reasoning in contemporaneous documentation, the limitations of population-based scoring systems and benchmarks, and the influence of resource availability on feasible treatment options. These principles were integrated into a structured framework for adverse-event review aimed at supporting proportionate analysis of adverse outcomes and avoiding premature attribution of individual blame when harm reflects interacting clinical, cognitive, team-level, and system-level factors.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Accountability in emergency surgery should evaluate decisions according to the information, physiological condition, reasonable alternatives, and resources available at the time of care. Contextualization should not eliminate individual responsibility; rather, it should make responsibility attribution more accurate, proportionate, and fair. A bias-aware, procedurally fair, and high-reliability approach can protect surgeons from premature, punitive, outcome-driven blame while preserving legitimate accountability for unsafe practice, reckless conduct, or misconduct. Such a framework may strengthen patient safety, professional integrity, organizational learning, and public trust.

articles.title: Evolution of surgical indication strategies and their impact on treatment outcomes in acute superior mesenteric venous thrombosis: a single-center retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: To compare how different surgical indication strategies affect treatment patterns and outcomes in patients with acute superior mesenteric vein thrombosis (SMVT), and to identify independent risk factors for intestinal wall full-thickness necrosis and in-hospital mortality.

**METHODS**: We retrospectively analyzed 125 patients with acute intestinal ischemia secondary to SMVT from October 2014 to October 2025. Patients were divided into two chronological cohorts according to the change in surgical indication strategy implemented at our institution: the liberal surgical indication period (October 2014 - October 2023, n = 102) and the strict surgical indication period (November 2023 - October 2025, n = 23). Baseline characteristics, treatment pathways, and in-hospital outcomes were compared between the two periods. Multivariate logistic regression was used to identify independent risk factors for in-hospital mortality and for full-thickness necrosis in patients undergoing surgery.

**RESULTS**: The two periods were comparable with respect to baseline characteristics (P > 0.05). Compared with the liberal period, the strict period had significantly lower rates of early surgery (4.3% vs. 63.7%, P < 0.001) and overall surgery (26.1% vs. 80.4%, P < 0.001). Full-thickness necrosis was identified in a significantly higher proportion of surgical specimens in the strict period than in the liberal period (83.3% vs. 18.3%, P = 0.002). Patients in the strict period had a longer median hospital stay (19 days vs. 12 days, P = 0.011), a trend toward lower ICU admission (30.4% vs. 50.0%, P = 0.089), and no significant difference in mortality (13.0% vs. 7.8%, P = 0.423). Multivariate analysis showed that lactate ≥ 4 mmol/L (aOR = 7.545, 95%CI: 1.827-31.149, P = 0.005) and elevated D-dimer (aOR = 1.047, 95%CI: 1.012-1.084, P = 0.008) were independently associated with in-hospital mortality. Given the limited number of death events (n = 11), the above multivariate analysis results should be considered exploratory findings that require validation in larger prospective cohorts. In surgical patients, CT evidence of impaired bowel wall perfusion independently predicted pathologically confirmed full-thickness necrosis (aOR = 6.236, 95%CI: 1.663-23.388, P = 0.007).

**CONCLUSION**: A strict surgical indication strategy with an anticoagulation-first approach was associated with a lower rate of surgery in SMVT patients and directs surgical intervention more precisely to those with established full-thickness necrosis. CT evidence of impaired bowel wall perfusion is a key warning sign for full-thickness necrosis and warrants urgent surgical evaluation. Hyperlactatemia and elevated D-dimer independently predict in-hospital mortality and should serve as core elements for early risk assessment and dynamic monitoring.

articles.title: Plasma eMTBR-tau as a Biomarker for Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy Tau Tangle Neuropathology.
articles.abstract:
**IMPORTANCE**: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) is a neurodegenerative disease that cannot accurately be diagnosed during life due to the absence of in vivo biomarkers for CTE neuropathology.

**OBJECTIVE**: To evaluate plasma endogenously cleaved microtubule-binding region tau (eMTBR-tau) as a candidate biomarker for CTE tau tangle neuropathology.

**DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS**: This case series included 21 former American-style football players who completed a blood draw as part of participation in clinical research at Boston University beginning April 17, 2008, and who subsequently died, donated their brain, and had completed autopsy by October 9, 2026.

**EXPOSURES**: Plasma eMTBR-tau nucleic acid-linked immunosandwich assay single-plex immunoassay and plasma phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217) (SP-X n = 20; Elecsys n = 1).

**MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES**: CTE status and stage. Cumulative neuropathologic tau burden scores ranged from 0 to 33 (higher scores indicate tau burden; 0, no tau burden).

**RESULTS**: Among 21 male brain donors (median age at blood draw, CTE positive: 68 years [IQR, 61-77]; CTE negative: 49 years [IQR, 47-56]), 18 had a neuropathologic diagnosis of CTE. Of these participants, 16 had a diagnosis of high-stage CTE (stage IV = 8, stage III = 8); and 2, of low-stage CTE (stage II = 1, stage I = 1). Five CTE-positive participants had intermediate or high Alzheimer disease neuropathologic change (ADNC). Plasma eMTBR-tau concentration was significantly higher in CTE-positive participants (median, 0.019 pg/mL [IQR, 0.004-0.030]) compared with CTE-negative participants (0.001 pg/mL [IQR, 0.001-0.001]; β = 1.61 [95% CI, 0.51-2.70]). Plasma eMTBR-tau concentrations were highest among CTE-positive participants with comorbid ADNC (0.082 pg/mL [IQR, 0.059-0.131]) and intermediate among those with high-stage CTE without ADNC (n = 11; median, 0.009 pg/mL [IQR, 0.004-0.021]). Plasma eMTBR-tau concentration was significantly higher in high-stage CTE (median, 0.021 pg/mL [IQR, 0.006-0.038]) compared with low-stage CTE (median, 0.001 pg/mL [IQR, 0.001-0.002]; β = 1.79 [95% CI, 0.45-3.13]) or no CTE (median, 0.001 pg/mL [IQR, 0.001-0.001]; β = 1.78 [95% CI, 0.85-2.71]). Differences remained significant after exclusion of 5 cases with comorbid ADNC. Plasma eMTBR-tau concentration was associated with higher cumulative neuropathologic tau burden score across 11 brain regions (β = 0.71 [95% CI, 0.38-1.05]). Plasma p-tau217 concentration was positively associated with eMTBR-tau (β = 0.68 [95% CI, 0.32-1.04]) but was not associated with CTE. P-tau217 concentrations were in the negative range (n = 11) or intermediate range (n = 5) for participants without ADNC copathology. Four participants with ADNC had p-tau217 concentrations in the positive range; and 1, in the intermediate range.

**CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE**: Participants with high-stage CTE had higher concentrations of plasma eMTBR-tau than those with low-stage or no CTE; concentrations were highest among those with CTE and comorbid ADNC. Plasma eMTBR-tau may represent a feasible biomarker candidate for high-stage CTE tau tangle neuropathology. Larger autopsy and clinical validation studies are needed to establish overall diagnostic accuracy and specificity of plasma eMTBR-tau for CTE neuropathology, in addition to the associated prognostic and clinical implications.

articles.title: What's Blood Got to Do with It? Identifying MPDS® Dispatch Codes Most Commonly Associated with Prehospital Blood Administration.
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVES**: This study aimed to identify Medical Priority Dispatch System (MPDS®) codes most frequently associated with prehospital blood utilization.

**METHODS**: We examined Delaware's prehospital blood database to determine dispatch codes where low titer group O positive whole blood (LTOWB) was administered. We calculated the number of blood units under each dispatch code within the study period (May 2023- February 2026). Using this data, we identified the MPDS® codes associated with the highest number of blood units, including the top five codes overall, top medical codes, and as well as blood utilization rates for penetrating versus blunt traumas.

**RESULTS**: The most frequent blood utilization came from the following dispatch codes: 29D02 (traffic collision, high mechanism) 32 patients, 27D04G (penetrating trauma with central wounds) 32 patients, 29D02M (auto versus pedestrian) 28 patients, 29D05 (traffic collision with entrapment) 24 patients, and 29D02L (auto versus bicycle/motorcycle) 20 patients. These five dispatch codes accounted for 29% of all prehospital LTOWB utilized within the 33-month study period. Analyzing blood utilization for non-traumatic dispatch codes revealed: 21D04/21D04M (dangerous hemorrhage, medical) 18 patients, 21D03/21D03M (hemorrhage, not alert, medical) 13 patients, 9E01/M9E01/M9E02 (cardiac or respiratory arrest/death, not breathing) 13 patients, and 21D05/21D05M (hemorrhage, abnormal breathing, medical) 7 patients. These four dispatch codes accounted for 11% (51 patients) of LTOWB utilization. When performing odds ratio analysis to determine odds of blood administration, we found 27D04G, 29D02M, and 29D02L to be statistically significant with 95% confidence intervals of [0.35- 0.87], [2.42- 5.72], [1.47- 3.91], and odds ratios of 0.55, 3.72, and 2.40, respectively. Additionally, our analysis demonstrated that patients with MPDS® coding for penetrating trauma with a delta level priority (27D) have higher likelihood of prehospital blood administration than delta priority high mechanism traffic incidents (29D). This comparison showed an OR of 10.40 that blood would be given to the penetrating trauma patient with a 95% confidence interval of [7.93- 13.66].

**CONCLUSIONS**: Specific MPDS® codes are strongly associated with prehospital blood utilization. Identifying these patterns offers a unique opportunity for emergency medical services systems to implement automatic blood dispatch protocols based on dispatch code.

articles.title: Prolonged Onboard Storage of Red Blood Cells in Ground Ambulances for Prehospital Transfusion: A Real-World Study.
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVES**: Permanent onboard storage of red blood cells (RBC) units could facilitate timely prehospital transfusion but may expose blood products to cumulative transport-related mechanical stress. We evaluated the quality of RBC units stored continuously in operational ground ambulances under real-world emergency medical service conditions.

**METHODS**: In this randomized controlled experimental study of RBC units, leukoreduced RBC units were randomly assigned to continuous onboard ambulance storage from day 7 to day 42 (

**RESULTS**: All RBC units remained below the European regulatory hemolysis threshold of 0.8% at day 42. Hemolysis was higher in ambulance-stored units at day 28 (Hodges-Lehmann difference, +0.043 percentage points; 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.010-0.076; 

**CONCLUSIONS**: Continuous onboard RBC storage in operational ground ambulances maintained all units within regulatory hemolysis limits through day 42. However, higher hemolysis and late divergence in SME accumulation suggest that prolonged ambulance exposure may influence RBC storage quality. These findings provide preliminary support for the feasibility of continuous onboard RBC storage, particularly earlier in the storage period, but do not establish equivalence with conventional blood bank storage.

articles.title: Early arthroplasty versus conversion arthroplasty after failed PFNA in elderly patients with unstable intertrochanteric fractures: a multicenter matched cohort study.
articles.abstract:
**PURPOSE**: In our study, the clinical and functional outcomes of early arthroplasty versus late conversion arthroplasty approaches were compared in individuals over 75 years of age who underwent PFNA for complex intertrochanteric fractures but whose treatment failed.

**METHODS**: This multicenter, retrospective cohort study analyzed data from 136 patients treated between January 2023 and March 2025. The cohort consisted of 62 patients who underwent conversion arthroplasty after failed PFNA fixation and 74 patients who received primary early arthroplasty. Demographic characteristics, surgical parameters, complications, and functional and rehabilitation outcomes were compared between groups.

**RESULTS**: Early arthroplasty was associated with significantly better six-month functional outcomes, including higher Parker mobility and Merle d'Aubigné scores. The early arthroplasty group also demonstrated shorter times to effective weight-bearing and recovery of walking distance. Perioperative transfusion requirements and systemic complication rates were higher in the PFNA conversion group. However, the time to recovery of unassisted gait did not differ significantly between groups.

**CONCLUSION**: Conclusion In elderly patients over 75 years of age with unstable intertrochanteric fractures, early arthroplasty was associated with better short-term functional outcomes, earlier effective weight-bearing and recovery of walking distance, and fewer systemic complications than conversion arthroplasty following failed PFNA. However, these findings should be interpreted in the context of the retrospective design and the functional deterioration that occurred between initial PFNA and subsequent conversion surgery. Primary arthroplasty may be a reasonable option in carefully selected patients with fracture patterns, poor bone quality, or clinical characteristics associated with a high risk of fixation failure.

articles.title: Prehospital Trauma Compendium: Prehospital Management of Pediatric Traumatic Out-of-Hospital Circulatory Arrest - A Joint Position Statement and Resource Document of NAEMSP, ACS-COT, ACEP, and AAP.
articles.abstract: In 2014 the National Association of EMS Physicians (NAEMSP), American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma (ACS-COT), American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP), and American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) published the first joint position statement discussing withholding and discontinuing resuscitation attempts for pediatric traumatic out-of-hospital circulatory arrest (TOHCA). Since then, the body of literature addressing pediatric TOHCA has evolved and evidence has grown that demonstrates the nearly uniformly poor prognosis of children who suffer circulatory arrest in the prehospital setting as a result of trauma. To support emergency medical services (EMS) clinicians in their approach to these high-acuity, low-frequency, and challenging cases, this project aimed to update guidance regarding decisions to withhold or discontinue resuscitation efforts for pediatric traumatic circulatory arrest. NAEMSP, ACEP, ACS-COT, and AAP recommend:EMS resuscitation of pediatric TOHCA should:Prioritize prompt identification of patients who may benefit from transport to definitive care at trauma centers when safe and appropriate. On-scene resuscitation should be balanced against the potential benefit of transfer to a proximate trauma center.Emphasize the identification of reversible causes of traumatic circulatory arrest and timely use of clinically indicated life-saving interventions (LSIs) within the EMS clinician's scope of practice. These include:External hemorrhage control with direct pressure, wound packing, and tourniquetsAirway management using the least-invasive airway interventions required to achieve and maintain airway patency, oxygenation, and adequate ventilation.Chest decompression if clinical concern for tension pneumothorax. Empiric bilateral decompression is not recommended in the absence of suspected thoracic trauma.External chest compressions and ventilations have a larger role in pediatric TOHCA resuscitation than in adult TOHCA resuscitation, with children frequently having TOHCA secondary to head injury, hypoxia and other non-hemorrhagic mechanisms. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) should be provided when the cause of circulatory arrest is unclear.Epinephrine is of lower priority than other LSIs.Consider point of care ultrasound (POCUS) to guide decisions to withhold or discontinue resuscitation efforts.Resuscitation attempts may be withheld in pediatric TOHCA patients with:Injuries that are incompatible with life (e.g., decapitation, hemi-corpectomy, incineration).Evidence of prolonged circulatory arrest (e.g., rigor mortis, dependent lividity, decomposition).Advanced care planning documents that indicate Do Not Resuscitate (DNR)/ Do Not Attempt Resuscitation (DNAR)/Allow Natural Death medical orders.Resuscitation attempts may be discontinued in pediatric TOHCA patients who:Have no return of spontaneous circulation after provision of at least 15 minutes of high-quality CPR in addition to performance of other lifesaving interventions directed at treating potentially reversible causes of pediatric TOHCA. Longer durations of CPR, up to 30 minutes, may be considered for patients with positive predictors of survival such as organized rhythm, witnessed arrest, bystander CPR, or with proximate access to a trauma center.Have known predictors of very low probability of survival such as penetrating trauma without proximate access to a trauma center, asystole, unwitnessed arrest, or lack of bystander CPR.Protocols guiding decisions to withhold or discontinue resuscitation of pediatric TOHCA benefit from oversight by EMS physicians in collaboration with pediatric experts and local or regional trauma system stakeholders. Implementation of such protocols for pediatric patients benefits from involvement of community stakeholders including family representatives, law enforcement, medical examiner, and child fatality review committees.Considerations for protocol implementation include local resource availability, EMS clinician and public safety, psychosocial support to surviving family members and emergency responders, and dignified handling of the deceased patient.Training needs for EMS clinicians include techniques to communicate with family members regarding the death of a child and understanding the clinician's own response to this low-frequency, high-emotion experience.

articles.title: Prevalence and Characteristics of Coma in Latin American Critical Care Units: The COMA LATAM Study.
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVES**: To determine the point prevalence of coma across Latin American critical care units, characterize its etiology, and explore short-term outcomes.

**DESIGN**: Multinational, cross-sectional point prevalence study with exploratory 14-day follow-up assessment.

**SETTING**: Three hundred ninety-two hospitals across 19 Latin American countries, including ICUs, intermediate care units, neurocritical care units, cardiovascular ICUs, and trauma ICUs.

**PATIENTS**: Adult patients (≥ 18 yr) meeting the Coma Epidemiology, Evaluation, and Therapy care survey (COME-TOGETHER) criteria on May 28, 2024. Patients under deep sedation or pharmacological coma induction were excluded unless the coma state preceded pharmacological intervention.

**INTERVENTIONS**: None (observational study).

**MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS**: Among 8305 critically ill patients, 1145 met coma criteria (point prevalence 13.8%), with country-specific rates ranging from 5.1% to 36.8%. Individual patient data were available for 729 patients (63.7%). Traumatic brain injury was the leading individual cause (24.8%), followed by hypoxic-anoxic brain injury (14.6%) and intracerebral hemorrhage (13.5%). When categorized by pathophysiology, vascular causes predominated (48.6%), followed by traumatic brain injury (24.8%) and other causes (26.6%). Age-stratified analysis revealed trauma predominantly affecting younger patients, while cerebrovascular causes predominated in older groups. Among patients with 14-day follow-up data (29% of cohort), mortality was 29.2%, with 67.7% of survivors recovering from coma. Only the Charlson Comorbidity Index was independently associated with implementation of life-sustaining therapy limitations (adjusted odds ratio, 1.22; 95% CI, 1.15-1.30; p < 0.001).

**CONCLUSIONS**: Coma affects nearly one in seven ICU beds across Latin America, with substantial country variation and distinct age-dependent etiology patterns. The significant burden highlights the need for targeted prevention strategies and specialized neurocritical care resources throughout the region.

articles.title: Trauma Clinician Perspectives on Geriatric-Centered Trauma Care: A Qualitative Study.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Despite national geriatric trauma guidelines, care delivery varies across trauma centers, and existing quality measures may not capture outcomes important to older injured adults. We examined clinician perspectives on geriatric-centered care structures, processes, and implementation barriers.

**STUDY DESIGN**: We conducted a descriptive, exploratory qualitative study of US trauma clinicians between September 2022 and December 2024. Semi-structured interviews explored geriatric trauma care delivery and clinician-reported outcomes. Transcripts underwent deductive analysis using the Donabedian quality framework and inductive thematic analysis using an adapted socioecological model.

**RESULTS**: Twenty-six clinicians from 23 trauma centers participated; 22 (85%) were surgeons, 25 (96%) practiced at Level I trauma centers, and 24 (92%) worked in academic hospitals. Participants identified 7 geriatric-centered structures, 21 care processes, and 11 outcomes considered important for assessing geriatric trauma care. Four themes emerged: variation in geriatric care structures and pathways across hospitals; financial, staffing, and organizational constraints; evolving professional identity and ownership of geriatric trauma care; and gaps in measuring outcomes important to older adults. Although clinicians described implementing selected components of national guidelines, no common comprehensive care model emerged. Participants emphasized that conventional hospital-based metrics inadequately capture postdischarge recovery, particularly functional status, independence, and quality of life.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Trauma clinicians reported substantial variation in geriatric-centered care, shaped by institutional resources, organizational priorities, and professional culture. Limited measurement of patient-centered, longitudinal outcomes constrains evaluation of geriatric trauma care. Incorporating functional recovery and quality of life into trauma quality assessment may help identify effective care structures and processes.

articles.title: A Novel Surgical Technique for Post-traumatic Syringomyelia Progressing to the Medulla Oblongata: Evidence of Upward Drainage of Central Canal Fluid Within the Spinal Cord: Corrigendum.
Endotracheal intubation practices, success rates and adverse events in four Dutch emergency departments: a multicentre retrospective study.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Endotracheal intubation in the emergency department (ED) is a high-risk intervention associated with significant complications. Contemporary European data on emergency airway management remain limited, and no published data are available from the Netherlands. This study aimed to describe endotracheal intubation practices, success rates, and adverse events in four Dutch EDs.

**METHODS**: We conducted a multicentre retrospective cohort study of patients undergoing endotracheal intubation in four teaching hospital EDs in the Netherlands between January 2019 and December 2023. Patients were identified using procedure registrations, diagnostic codes, billing information and disposition records. Trained abstractors collected standardized data on patient characteristics, indications, provider characteristics, intubation techniques, medications, first-pass success and adverse events.

**RESULTS**: A total of 1250 intubations were included. The most common indication was post-return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) after cardiac arrest (47%), followed by neurologic pathology (14%), cardiac arrest (12%), respiratory insufficiency (8%), intoxication (8%), and trauma (5%). Emergency medicine and intensive care physicians performed most intubations. Videolaryngoscopy was the primary technique in 89.5% of cases, and etomidate was the most frequently used induction agent (73.5%). The overall first-pass success rate was 93.8% and did not differ by provider specialty or level of training. Adverse events occurred in 181 patients (14.5%), with hypotension (6.5%) and desaturation (4.7%) being most common. Increasing age (OR 1.07 per year, 95% CI 1.04-1.10) and cardiac pathology as indication for intubation (OR 3.50, 95% CI 1.03-11.88) were associated with hypotension. A higher body mass index (OR 1.08 per point, 95% CI 1.03-1.13), younger age (OR 0.98 per year, 95% CI 0.96-1.00, p = 0.022) and multiple intubations attempts (OR 2.9, 95% CI 1.12-7.33) were associated with desaturation. Lower pre-intubation oxygen saturation was associated with peri-intubation cardiac arrest (OR 0.96 per point, 95% CI 0.92-0.99).

**CONCLUSIONS**: This study provides the first multicentre description of emergency airway management in Dutch EDs and demonstrates a distinctive emergency intubation population, characterised by a high proportion of post-ROSC intubations. Contemporary practice was characterised by widespread adoption of videolaryngoscopy, frequent use of etomidate, and high first-pass success rates. Peri-intubation hypotension and desaturation remained common and represent important targets for quality improvement.

**TRIAL REGISTRATION**: clinicaltrials.gov NCT06374030.
articles.journal: Scand J Trauma Resusc Emerg Med

articles.title: Predicting mortality in pediatric cases with severe traumatic brain injury: is the Eppendorf-Cologne Scale more reliable than Glasgow Coma Scale?
articles.abstract:
**PURPOSE**: Severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) in children is a major cause of morbidity and mortality, requiring reliable tools for early assessment and prognosis. While the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is the standard neurological evaluation tool, it has limitations in pediatric patients. The Eppendorf-Cologne Scale (ECS), originally developed for adults, emphasizes pupil size, reactivity, and motor response and may offer advantages in children.

**METHODS**: This multicenter cohort study analyzed TraumaRegister DGU

**RESULTS**: Among the cohort, 2,582 patients (44.1%) had severe TBI and 476 (8.1%) died in hospital. GCS showed slightly higher accuracy for predicting severe TBI (AUROC 0.778, 95% CI 0.766-0.791) than ECS (AUROC 0.745, 95% CI 0.731-0.758). For mortality prediction, ECS performed marginally better (AUROC 0.943, 95% CI 0.929-0.957) than GCS (AUROC 0.910, 95% CI 0.896-0.924). Mortality rates were 90% in the worst ECS category and 55% in the worst GCS category.

**CONCLUSION**: GCS showed higher discrimination for severe TBI, whereas ECS showed higher discrimination for in-hospital mortality among patients with severe TBI. ECS may provide complementary prognostic information, but its clinical utility and role alongside GCS require prospective evaluation.

articles.title: Blunt anatomical cardiac injury (BACI) - lessons from a single trauma center cohort.
articles.abstract:
**INTRODUCTION**: Patients with anatomical damage to the heart after blunt trauma are rarely seen in hospital settings due to their elevated prehospital mortality. The aim of this study is to review our center experience with this entity.

**METHODS**: After institutional research board approval, a local Trauma Databank search (Qatar National Trauma Registry) was performed from 2016 to 2025. Cases presented with blunt trauma and anatomical changes to pericardium or heart, detected in imaging or surgery, in patients above 13 years old were diagnosed as blunt anatomical cardiac injury - BACI and included.

**RESULTS**: Amongst 17542 blunt trauma cases admitted to our Trauma Center during the study period, 15 patients (0.09% incidence) met the inclusion/exclusion criteria. All patients were males, with average age of 43 years (ranges 26-75), with ISS of 32 (ranges 10-75). The most common mechanism of injury was pedestrian struck (5cases -33%). Hypotension at trauma room assessment was common (8 cases - 53% of patients) and 8 patients (53%) required surgery. FAST, echocardiogram and computed tomography were used as diagnostic tools. The patients presented in 4 anatomical patterns: (a) intracardiac/valve damage; (b) pericardial effusion; (c) pericardial laceration and (d) cardiac rupture. Three patients (20%) died, all during emergent surgery and sustaining cardiac rupture.

**CONCLUSION**: BACI is uncommonly seen at Emergency Departments and carries elevated early mortality in cases with cardiac rupture, requiring high index of suspicion for diagnosis. Different clinical presentations of BACI were observed and described in this series. Further studies with larger number of patients are needed to further clarify possible differences in severity, surgical requirement and mortality according to the BACI structural presentation.

articles.title: Management of Traumatic Pneumothorax in the Emergency Department: A Two-Centre Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVE**: To describe clinical characteristics, initial emergency department (ED) management strategy (conservative or chest drain) and outcomes of patients who present to the ED with traumatic pneumothorax.

**METHODS**: Retrospective cohort study of patients aged 14 years and older with an ED diagnosis of traumatic pneumothorax between January 2023 and March 2025 in two EDs. Pleural intervention was defined as needle decompression, thoracostomy, or chest drain. Descriptive data are reported, and logistic regression was used to identify predictors of ED-initiated chest drain insertion.

**RESULTS**: Of 339 eligible patients, 50 had a pre-hospital pleural intervention, of which 27 had chest drains inserted to formalise (finger) thoracostomy or needle decompression. A further 58 patients received an ED-initiated chest drain, for a total of 85 ED chest drains (25.1%). Of the 231 (68.1%) who were initially managed conservatively, 53 received a drain during their hospital stay, primarily as part of surgical management. The majority (71.9%) of drains were large-bore (≥ 24 Fr). Predictors of ED-initiated pleural drainage were: pneumothorax size > 35 mm (aOR 41.0, 95% CI 16.4-102) and presence of haemothorax (aOR 6.3, 95% CI 2.5-15.8). Thirty-six drained patients (22.8%) had a recorded complication. In-hospital mortality was 5.6%.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Two-thirds of patients with traumatic pneumothorax were initially managed without drainage before departing the ED. Later drainage frequently reflected operative or broader trauma management rather than clinical deterioration. Pneumothorax size and haemothorax were independent factors associated with ED-initiated drainage. The predominance of large-bore drains and frequency of complications identify opportunities for structured selective management and drain-selection pathways.

articles.title: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome.
articles.abstract: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a common cause of acute hypoxemic respiratory failure in patients with pneumonia, sepsis, aspiration of gastric contents, severe trauma, or other inciting triggers. Although the definition of the syndrome has evolved over the past several decades, the core elements (acute onset, hypoxemia, and bilateral radiographic opacities) remain consistent. Critical components of management include identification and treatment of the underlying cause of ARDS as well as avoidance of ventilator-induced lung injury and volume overload. Ongoing areas of controversy include the best strategy for supporting nonintubated patients, personalization of positive end-expiratory pressure, the role of innovative ventilatory strategies, and the use of glucocorticoids. New research suggests that precision medicine approaches to ARDS management that focus on discrete biologic, radiographic, or physiological subphenotypes may improve outcomes, and prospective trials of these approaches are ongoing.

articles.title: Hospital-Based Violence Intervention and Fragmentation of Trauma Care.
ICU Mortality Associated With Clinically Important Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding: A Multistate Analysis.
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVES**: Clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding may increase mortality and time to discharge from the ICU. Conventional analyses ignore timing and treat bleeding as a binary event. We evaluated the association between time-dependent clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding and ICU mortality.

**DESIGN AND SETTING**: A multicenter cohort study using data from an international stress ulcer prophylaxis trial.

**PATIENTS**: A total of 4821 invasively ventilated adult participants.

**INTERVENTIONS**: None.

**MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS**: A multistate model was specified with two transient ICU states (bleed-free and post-bleed) and four absorbing states (ICU discharge or death, each with or without bleeding). The Aalen-Johansen method was used to estimate transition and state occupancy probabilities and to describe risks of different clinical courses. Follow-up was censored at 90 days. We fit two Cox models for time to death in the ICU regressing on time-dependent bleeding history while adjusting for age, sex, baseline Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II score, admission category (medical/surgical/trauma), vasopressor/inotrope use and renal replacement therapy on study day 1 and randomized allocation of pantoprazole or placebo; a second model also adjusted for time-dependent covariates of advanced life support (invasive mechanical ventilation, vasopressor/inotrope use, and renal replacement therapy). Clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding developed in 104 patients (2.2%) in the ICU. Median ICU length of stay for those who experienced bleeding was 19 days (interquartile range [IQR], 11-30 d) vs. 9 days (IQR, 5-15 d) for those who did not. Accounting for immortal time bias, the time-dependent indicator of clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding was associated with increased ICU mortality (hazard ratio, 1.56; 95% CI, 1.13-2.15). At any time, patients who experienced bleeding had approximately 1.6 times the hazard of ICU mortality compared with those without a history of bleeding.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding as a time-dependent event is associated with an increased risk of ICU mortality.

articles.title: Propranolol administration following traumatic brain injury induces distinct neuroinflammatory gene expression profiles.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains a major cause of morbidity and is frequently followed by prolonged intensive care stays with sustained physiologic stress. Beta-blockade has been investigated as an adjunct therapy for TBI given its potential to reduce sympathetic hyperactivation. The molecular mechanisms underlying neuroinflammatory signaling remain incompletely defined. We hypothesized that propranolol (BB) administration following TBI would modify neuroinflammatory transcriptional responses consistent with attenuation of maladaptive inflammatory signaling.

**METHODS**: Male Sprague-Dawley rats (n=6-8/group) were divided into 6 groups: (1) TBI7d (controlled cortical impact) followed by 7 days of daily handling, (2) TBI7d with daily propranolol administration (TBI BB7d), (3) TBI with chronic restraint stress for 7 days (TBI CRS7d), (4) TBI CRS7d with daily propranolol administration (TBI CRS BB7d), (5) CRS7d (n=7) who underwent daily stress exposure for 7 days; and (6) CRS BB7d (n=7) underwent daily stress exposure with propranolol injections for 7 days. RNA was extracted from the injured frontal lobe and analyzed using the NanoString Neuroinflammation panel. Differential gene expression was analyzed using ROSALIND. Significant differentially expressed genes (sDEGs) were defined as fold change ≥1.5 or ≤-1.5 with p<0.05. Functional pathway analysis was performed using Qiagen Ingenuity Pathway Analysis.

**RESULTS**: Compared with TBI alone, TBI BB7d demonstrated 83 sDEGs, including genes associated with neuronal signaling, neurotransmitter regulation, and epigenetic modulation. Pathway analysis identified significant involvement of the IL8 signaling and FXR/RXR. In the TBI CRS7d model, propranolol treatment yielded 21 sDEGs. These genes were enriched in pathways related to cellular stress responses and inflammatory regulation. Propranolol downregulated IL6, IL8, and neuroinflammation signaling pathways.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Propranolol administration following TBI, with and without stress, resulted in distinct neuroinflammatory transcriptional profiles. Propranolol was associated with alterations in multiple pathways involved in stress response, immune regulation, and neurorecovery. These findings suggest beta-blockade may modulate stress-related neuroinflammatory signaling following TBI.

articles.title: The Radiographic Lung Edema Score in Pediatric Acute Respiratory Failure: Associations With Systemic Inflammatory Biomarkers and Multiple Organ Dysfunction.
articles.abstract:
**OBJECTIVES**: Although chest radiographs (CXR) are among the most used imaging modalities in critically ill patients, their interpretation and clinical significance remain incompletely leveraged. The Radiographic Lung Edema (RALE) score is a prognostic bedside tool widely applied in adults to quantify lung edema on CXR. However, this score has been infrequently studied in children, and its potential to reflect broader aspects of critical illness pathophysiology beyond the lungs is unknown. We sought to determine the reproducibility of the RALE score, and whether higher RALE scores were associated with circulating inflammatory and endothelial biomarkers, multi-organ dysfunction, and worse clinical outcomes in pediatric acute respiratory failure (ARF).

**DESIGN**: Retrospective cohort study.

**SETTING**: Multicenter PICUs.

**PATIENTS**: Critically ill children (2 wk to 17 yr old) receiving invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) for ARF, enrolled in the CAF-PINT (Coagulation and Fibrinolysis in Pediatric Insulin Titration) study (2012-2016).

**INTERVENTIONS**: None.

**MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS**: A baseline RALE score was calculated for each patient from a single CXR obtained within 72 hours of IMV initiation. Among 212 patients, RALE scores demonstrated good inter-rater reliability (intra-class coefficient 0.85; 95% CI, 0.82-0.87). After adjustment for ARF etiology and illness severity, higher RALE scores were associated with fewer 28-day ventilator-free days (sub-distribution hazard ratio per 1-sd increase, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.69-0.95). Structural equation modeling demonstrated that this association was mediated through both pulmonary dysfunction, measured by the oxygenation index (β -0.14; 95% bootstrapped CI, -0.22 to -0.06), and extrapulmonary organ dysfunction, measured by the Pediatric Logistic Organ Dysfunction score (β -0.05; 95% bootstrapped CI, -0.10 to -0.002). Similar associations were observed for 28-day PICU-free days. Finally, penalized regression selected soluble triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells-1, intercellular adhesion molecule-1, and tumor necrosis factor receptor-1 as biomarkers associated with higher RALE scores.

**CONCLUSIONS**: We provide evidence that the RALE score is not solely a lung injury marker but also reflects broader systemic pathophysiology. These findings have important implications for the interpretation and clinical application of this bedside tool in pediatric ARF.

articles.title: State Variation in Crime Victim Compensation Denials after Violent Injury in the United States.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Crime victim compensation (CVC) can offset financial burdens after violent injury, yet state-level administrative requirements may restrict access. We examined variation in CVC denials and associations with modifiable program policies.

**STUDY DESIGN**: This cross-sectional study analyzed Office for Victims of Crime administrative data from all 50 states and Washington, D.C., for fiscal year 2023. State program characteristics and socioeconomic vulnerability were evaluated against application denial rates using multivariable beta regression. Hierarchical clustering identified denial-reason profiles; leave-one-state-out analyses assessed robustness.

**RESULTS**: Across 51 programs, denial rates ranged from 3.9% to 75% (median 25%; IQR, 14%-39%). States permitting exemptions from law enforcement reporting had lower denial rates than states requiring reporting (OR 0.56; 95% CI, 0.34-0.93; p=0.024). Higher state-level socioeconomic vulnerability was associated with higher denial rates (OR 5.5; 95% CI, 1.5-20; p=0.009). Incomplete information (26%) and ineligible applications (24%) were the leading denial reasons. The administrative-barrier cluster encompassed 27 states and had the highest mean denial rate (34.4%), compared with 17.1% in the behavioral-scrutiny cluster (p=0.04 for pairwise comparison). Reporting-exemption associations retained their direction across all 51 leave-one-state-out models and remained statistically significant in 50.

**CONCLUSIONS**: CVC denial rates vary markedly across states and are associated with law enforcement reporting policies and socioeconomic vulnerability. Administrative documentation barriers characterize states with higher denial rates. Expanding reporting exemptions and integrating application navigation into trauma care warrant evaluation as strategies to improve access to post-injury financial assistance.

articles.title: Shift change: 12- versus 24-hour work period models in acute care surgery.
Nursing led protocols in trauma: a point-counterpoint analysis.
articles.abstract: This narrative point-counterpoint analysis examines the benefits, risks, and implementation requirements of nursing-led medication administration protocols in trauma and emergency care. It draws on the debate at the 2026 Maryland Committee on Trauma Point/Counterpoint XLIII Conference in Baltimore and selected published literature to develop practical recommendations for clinical use and evaluation. The conference proposition that these protocols save lives is examined critically; this article does not report an original outcomes study. Reported benefits include earlier medication administration, improved symptom management, and more consistent delivery of indicated treatment. One randomized emergency department evaluation reported a 186-min reduction in median time to acetaminophen, and a retrospective intracerebral hemorrhage cohort associated nursing-led protocol changes with faster blood pressure control. These findings support improvements in care processes but do not establish a general survival benefit in trauma. Risks include inappropriate patient selection, medication errors, delayed escalation, and excessive protocol complexity. Safe implementation requires multidisciplinary agreement on scope, clear eligibility and exclusion criteria, accessible escalation pathways, and education that accounts for staff turnover and fatigue. Protocols should be integrated into trauma and emergency performance improvement processes to monitor adherence, treatment timeliness, adverse events, and patient outcomes, with feedback and reassessment after corrective action. Nursing-led medication protocols can improve timely care when supported by these safeguards; their effectiveness and sustainability require ongoing evaluation in the populations and settings where they are used.

articles.title: Should MAP augmentation remain the standard therapy after traumatic spinal cord injury?
articles.abstract: Traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI) remains one of the most devastating injuries in trauma care. For nearly three decades, maintenance of elevated mean arterial pressure (MAP) has been advocated to mitigate secondary ischemic injury after SCI and help preserve or improve neurologic outcomes. Although current guidelines continue to recommend augmentation of MAP and strict avoidance of hypotension, the supporting evidence remains predominantly observational. At the 41st Annual Point/counterpoint Acute Care Surgery Conference, experts debated whether MAP augmentation remains necessary after SCI. This review summarizes the physiologic rationale, supporting and opposing clinical evidence, emerging concepts in spinal cord perfusion pressure, and future directions in hemodynamic management. Level of evidence: III.

articles.title: Early Prehospital Prediction of Neurological Outcome After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Derivation and External Validation of the MIRA-29 Score.
articles.abstract:
**INTRODUCTION**: Out-of-hospital cardiac (OHCA) arrest is a frequent emergency, and few patients will survive with good neurological outcome. Identification of patients with a low likelihood of meaningful recovery represents a major clinical challenge. Numerous scores have been developed to guide decision-making after OHCA, with variable goals and targets, but most of them have been validated on small cohorts, integrates variables not available in the prehospital field, or do have low prediction values. MIRA-29 score aimed to only rely on simple clinical variables, available in the prehospital setting. We hypothetized that such score will provide incremental neurological prognosis value at an early-stage following OHCA.

**METHODS**: MIRA-29 score was derived and internally validated over a five-year period on a prospective cohort of 1099 adult patients, including all OHCA treated by our territory dispatch center. Multivariate analysis identified independent variables within the database, that were used to optimize the prediction model using machine-learning and genetic algorithms. The score was subsequently validated externally on 82 696 patients extracted from the French national cardiac arrest registry (RéAC).

**RESULTS**: Out from the 1099 patients, 85 patients (7.7%) had a favorable neurological outcome. Multivariate analysis identified five independent variables associated with neurological outcome: age, low-flow duration, number of external electric shock, epinephrine dose, and the OHCA site (street, public facility, home). After model optimization and machine-learning, age was not retained within the final model. External validation depicted a precision of 0.86 and a recall of 0.88 of the model. The F1-Score and accuracy are respectively 0.87 and 0.88, and specificity for a bad neurological prognosis is 0.99.

**CONCLUSION**: MIRA‑29 strength lies on its ability to reliably identify patients with extremely high probability of poor neurological outcome, while being based on four simple clinical variables. The prospective validation of MIRA-29 in the clinical setting may evaluate its impact on clinical decision making.

articles.title: RescQ
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Bystanders to out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) are at significant risk of psychological distress, yet no standardised support pathway exists for them in the UK. RescQ™ is a digital-first bystander support pathway embedded within regional prehospital and cardiac arrest care services.

**AIM**: To evaluate the feasibility of embedding RescQ™ into routine emergency medical services (EMS) practice leading to appropriate contact with bystanders involved in OHCA. Secondary aims were to describe digital access, demand for liaison officer (LO) support, identification of younger bystanders, and EMS clinician acceptability.

**METHODS**: Prospective one-year regional service evaluation of RescQ™ across Essex, UK. Bystanders involved in eligible OHCA events were registered by EMS clinicians and provided with immediate access to secure digital resources. Bystanders could self-refer for additional support through LO.

**RESULTS**: During the one-year evaluation, 220 of 432 eligible OHCA incidents had at least one bystander identified and the incident entered into the RescQ™ pathway, representing an incident-level capture rate of 50.9%. Across these incidents, 298 bystanders were identified, of whom 260 eligible adults were registered with RescQ™. Of registered adult bystanders, 96.2% accessed the digital resources at least once. Among all identified bystanders, 30/298 (10.1%) were aged under 18 years. Approximately 10% of registered bystanders self-referred for additional personalised LO support. Among 25 EMS clinician survey respondents who had used RescQ

**CONCLUSION**: RescQ™ demonstrated the feasibility of identifying and supporting bystanders following OHCA through a digitally enabled pathway, achieving incident-level capture above the pre-specified feasibility threshold and high website access among registered adults. These findings support further multi-region evaluation of implementation, sustainability and scalability across different EMS systems.

articles.title: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrests due to foreign body airway obstruction: A CanROC registry, retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Foreign body airway obstruction (FBAO) is a treatable cause of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but North American data are limited.

**METHODS**: Exploratory retrospective cohort study of EMS-treated OHCAs using the Canadian Resuscitation Outcomes Consortium (CanROC) registry (2005-2023), classified as obviously FBAO-related or of no obvious cause (presumed cardiac). Logistic regression compared Utstein characteristics between etiologies and identified factors associated with prehospital return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and survival to acute care discharge.

**RESULTS**: Among 105,178 EMS-treated OHCAs, 1,106(1.1%) were obviously FBAO-related. Compared with cases of no obvious cause, obviously FBAO-related cases were older (median 73 vs 68 years, p<0.001), more often witnessed (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 6.98[5.36-9.25]), more often attended by trained bystanders (aOR 3.30[2.41-4.41]), and less often had a shockable rhythm (aOR 0.11[0.07-0.15]). Obviously FBAO-related cases more often achieved prehospital ROSC (62.7% vs 37.8%; OR 2.77[2.44-3.13]), but survival did not differ (10.6% vs 9.0%,p=0.094). Within the obviously FBAO-related cohort, ROSC was associated with witnessed arrest (aOR 1.66[1.13-2.43]) and shorter EMS response time (aOR 0.95 per minute[0.92-0.99]). Survival was associated with younger age (aOR 0.76 per decade[0.61-0.93]), initial shockable rhythm (aOR 4.76[1.55-13.30]), and shorter EMS response time (aOR 0.81 per minute[0.66-0.98]). Survival was 18.1% and 0.8% among obviously FBAO-related OHCAs with and without prehospital ROSC, respectively.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Obviously FBAO-related OHCAs are uncommon but clinically distinct. ROSC is frequent, yet survival remains low and is associated with early prehospital factors, supporting choking prevention initiatives, bystander training, and rapid EMS response.

articles.title: Field Amputation by helicopter emergency service personnel: A cross-sectional survey of clinical practice and experience within air ambulance services in England.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Field Amputation (FA) is a rare, but potentially life-saving procedure undertaken by helicopter emergency medical services (HEMS) in the UK. Literature pertaining to FA predominantly originates from outside the UK, where the operational, clinical and legal differences make its applicability to the UK uncertain. Consequently, the severe lack of FA reports from the UK mean that FA is poorly documented in this setting. The aim is to establish the current prehospital FA clinical guidance and practice in the UK.

**METHOD/DISCUSSION**: An electronic, cross-sectional survey was sent to all UK HEMS. The survey sought to improve understanding of clinical practice, including service provision, scope of practice, equipment, training, governance and incidences of FA. Surveys were analysed with descriptive statistics and descriptive thematic analysis.

**RESULTS**: 15 HEMS responded, with 14 included for final analysis after one response was excluded. All respondents were from England. Every HEMS (n = 14, 100%) could provide FA, with 12 (86%) having a Clinical Practice Guideline specific to FA. Four services (29%) had undertaken FA within the last five years, totalling six cases, which were deemed notable given the absence of case reports from the UK in that time. A Gigli saw was the most popular instrument for bone disarticulation (n = 13, 93%). Unlike the USA and Korea, no respondents used hospital response teams to provide FA.

**CONCLUSION**: FA service provision is widely available across England, with cases of FA being undertaken, yet little standardisation nationally. A national or international registry of every FA case could provide further insights into this area of clinical practice.

articles.title: The epidemiology and burden of injury in The Gambia: A prospective trauma registry study.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Traumatic injury is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), yet robust prospective data characterizing injury epidemiology remain limited across sub-Saharan Africa. This study describes the demographic, injury, and initial treatment characteristics of patients enrolled in a hospital-based trauma registry in The Gambia. These data provide a foundation for characterizing the country's injury burden, guiding resource allocation, and informing continued trauma-system development.

**METHODS**: A prospective descriptive study was conducted using data from a hospital-based trauma registry established at Edward Francis Small Teaching Hospital, The Gambia's principal tertiary referral center for trauma and orthopaedic care. Injured patients presenting to the Trauma Emergency Unit from June 2022 through September 2025 were enrolled. Data included demographics, injury mechanism and setting, intent, anatomic injury location, injury type, and Trauma Emergency Unit disposition. Descriptive statistics were calculated.

**RESULTS**: Of 3380 enrolled patients, 76.1% were male, with a median age of 25 years. Most injuries occurred in villages (41.1%). Transport-related injuries were the leading mechanism (47.1%), followed by falls (29.3%) and violence/assault (21.4%). Streets/highways were the most common place of injury (43.3%), and nearly all injuries were unintentional (96.1%). The lower extremity below the knee (29.6%), head (22.3%), and hand (21.7%) were the most frequently injured body regions. Soft tissue injuries predominated (57.0%), followed by closed fractures (24.3%) and open fractures (11.7%). Overall, 55.9% of patients were discharged home, 29.3% were dispositioned to the operating theatre, and 10.1% left without being seen or before completing treatment. Among patients with recorded Trauma Emergency Unit disposition, 2.6% (n = 84) were categorized as 'mortuary or died.'

**CONCLUSIONS**: To our knowledge, this represents the largest prospective trauma registry analysis of injury epidemiology in The Gambia. Trauma disproportionately affected young males and was driven primarily by transport-related injuries, with a substantial burden occurring in rural settings. The frequency of fractures and incomplete treatment encounters highlights priorities for road-safety interventions, strengthened prehospital and referral systems, and expanded trauma, orthopaedic, and diagnostic capacity. Continued prospective trauma surveillance can support resource allocation, quality improvement, and national trauma-system development.

articles.title: Exposure technology and tissue protection in anterior and anterolateral thoracic/thoracolumbar fracture surgery: An international surgeon survey of retractor performance, mitigation strategies, and design priorities.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Anterior and anterolateral thoracic/thoracolumbar fracture surgery can provide direct vertebral-body and ventral canal access but requires controlled exposure through deep, anatomy-constrained corridors. We evaluated surgeon-reported retractor performance, tissue-protection behaviors, and device-design priorities.

**METHODS**: An international web-based survey was completed by 82 surgeons from 22 countries. Detailed analyses were restricted to 39 surgeons who reported personal anterior/anterolateral T4-L2 fracture surgery within 5 years. Likert items, multi-select mitigation strategies, and 26 free-text design responses were summarized descriptively; Rasch hierarchy, specialty differential item functioning (DIF), and MADQ3 residual correlations were exploratory response-structure analyses.

**RESULTS**: Standard rib spreaders, table-mounted ring retractors, and expandable lateral retractors were each used by 17/39 surgeons (43.6%). Prominent signals were large body habitus increasing difficulty and pressure (28/33, 84.8%), adjunct visualization (28/35, 80.0%), T11-L2 working distance (27/34, 79.4%), stability/minimal creep (26/37, 70.3%), and blade geometry (21/31, 67.7%). Common protective strategies were avoiding the inferior-rib neurovascular bundle (23/39, 59.0%), periodic partial release (20/39, 51.3%), and limiting blade opening according to imaging or chest-wall size (15/39, 38.5%). Overall soft-tissue risk (7/36, 19.4%) and reported complication frequency (1/33, 3.0%) had lower upper-category endorsement. Design responses prioritized blade geometry/pressure distribution (13/26, 50.0%), integrated illumination (12/26, 46.2%), and imaging/optical integration (11/26, 42.3%). No DIF signal survived false-discovery-rate correction.

**CONCLUSIONS**: Surgeons conceptualized safe exposure as a coupled mechanical, visual, and tissue-loading problem. Future retractor systems should be evaluated at depth for stability, pressure distribution, blade geometry, illumination, imaging compatibility, and workflow using objective bench and cadaveric metrics.

articles.title: Retrograde gearshift pedicle probe-assisted reduction of displaced superior pubic rami fractures: A technical note.
articles.abstract: Percutaneous fixation of superior pubic ramus fractures relies on establishment of safe corridors. Rotational and multiplanar deformity due to fracture disrupts the corridors and percutaneous or open reduction of these fractures is challenging. Retrograde insertion of a curved gearshift pedicle probe allows the surgeon to create a joystick to affect translation, rotation and angulation with a single instrument to restore the superior pubic ramus corridor and allow passage of an antegrade wire or screw. Following corridor restoration, reduction was captured antegrade, while definitive implant type and trajectory were selected independently according to fracture and osseous corridor morphology. Three displaced superior pubic ramus fractures were treated using this technique including mid-ramus, high ramus and segmental fractures with translational and rotational components. The probe was effectively used to de-rotate and reduce the fractures to allow for safe insertion of internal fixation with full containment and no complications. The curved gearshift pedicle probe is a rigid intramedullary reduction aid capable of multiplanar fragment manipulation and restoration of superior pubic ramus corridor while preserving independent selection of definitive fixation.

articles.title: Concomitant pelvic ring injury compromises acetabular reduction quality: A propensity score-matched analysis with surgical sequence subgroup study.
articles.abstract:
**BACKGROUND**: Concomitant pelvic ring injury is reported to compromise acetabular fracture reduction, yet matched comparisons are scarce and the optimal surgical sequence remains debated. We assessed whether pelvic ring injury compromises anatomical acetabular reduction, and whether fixation sequence influences reduction quality and complications.

**METHODS**: We retrospectively reviewed 119 consecutive patients with isolated displaced acetabular fractures and 20 patients with combined pelvic ring and acetabular injuries treated at a tertiary trauma center (2004-2023). One-to-one propensity score matching using age, sex, and Letournel classification yielded 20 matched pairs (n = 40). Within the combined group, eight patients underwent acetabulum-first and 12 underwent pelvic ring-first fixation. The primary outcome was anatomical acetabular reduction (modified Matta criteria, 0-1 mm) graded by two independent reviewers. Secondary outcomes were pelvic ring reduction and postoperative complications.

**RESULTS**: Anatomical acetabular reduction was achieved in 14 of 20 isolated patients (70.0%) versus four of 20 combined patients (20.0%; p = 0.004). Within combined injuries, acetabulum-first showed a numerical trend toward better reduction (37.5% vs 8.3% anatomical; p = 0.132). Pelvic ring reduction did not differ between sequence subgroups (75.0% vs 83.3%; p = 0.450).
